summary: Source decomposition of the Bhargava-Shankar 2-Selmer count from arXiv:1006.1002v3: the invariants I and J with their GL_2-weights, the height normalizations on forms and on curves and the eligibility congruences modulo 27 (ST.0); the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer/Cremona parametrization of 2-Selmer elements by locally soluble integral binary quartic forms with the stabilizer identification, and the auxiliary embedding into pairs of ternary quadratic forms (ST.1); the averaging formula over a non-compact fundamental domain, Davenport's lattice-point estimate, the cusp cutoff, and the uniformity estimate that licenses infinitely many congruence conditions (ST.2); the quoted quadratic and cubic predecessors (ST.3); and the theorem that the average size of the 2-Selmer group over any large family is 3, evaluated as the Tamagawa number of PGL_2 over Q, together with the convexity step giving average rank at most 1.5 (ST.4). Every result whose proof lies outside the source read is recorded as an unresolved import, including the entire parametrization. One supplier problem is recorded: the geometry-of-numbers input is Davenport's semialgebraic lattice-point lemma, not the Minkowski convex-body theorem supplied by GN.1, and no atlas stage owns it.

nodes.title: The invariants I and J, the height on binary quartic forms and on elliptic curves, and the eligible pairs
nodes.statement: For f(x,y) = a x^4 + b x^3 y + c x^2 y^2 + d x y^3 + e y^4 the ring of SL_2^{pm}(R)-invariants is generated by I(f) = 12ae - 3bd + c^2 (degree 2) and J(f) = 72ace + 9bcd - 27ad^2 - 27eb^2 - 2c^3 (degree 3), which are relative invariants for GL_2 with I(gamma f) = (det gamma)^4 I(f) and J(gamma f) = (det gamma)^6 J(f); the discriminant is Delta(f) = (4I(f)^3 - J(f)^2)/27 and the height is H(f) := H(I,J) = max{|I|^3, J^2/4}. Every elliptic curve over Q is isomorphic to a unique E_{A,B} : y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B with A, B integers and, for every prime p, p^6 not dividing B whenever p^4 | A; its naive height is H(E_{A,B}) = max{4|A^3|, 27B^2}, and with I(E) = -3A, J(E) = -27B one has H'(E) := max{|I(E)|^3, J(E)^2/4} and 27 H(E) = 4 H'(E), so H and H' induce the same ordering. A pair (I,J) in Z x Z occurs as the invariants of an integral binary quartic form (is ELIGIBLE) if and only if one of: I == 0 (mod 3) and J == 0 (mod 27); I == 1 (mod 9) and J == +-2 (mod 27); I == 4 (mod 9) and J == +-16 (mod 27); I == 7 (mod 9) and J == +-7 (mod 27).
hypotheses: The GL_2 action is by linear substitution gamma . f(x,y) = f((x,y) gamma), a LEFT action; a different convention changes the exponents in (5)
The minimality condition on the Weierstrass model is exactly 'p^4 | A implies p^6 does not divide B'; without it the model, and hence the height, is not unique
The two heights H and H' differ by the factor 27/4; every asymptotic constant depends on which is used, but the induced ordering is the same
Theorem 1.7 is an if-and-only-if characterization modulo 27 only; no other congruence conditions are needed
proofSteps: The invariants and their weights are computed directly from the classical invariant theory of the binary quartic (formulas (4) and (5)).
The discriminant, being a relative invariant of degree 6, is expressed in I and J as (4I^3 - J^2)/27.

Theorem 1.7 is proved in section 2.8 of the source (proof not read for this packet); its consequence recorded in the text is that the number of eligible (I,J) with H(I,J) < X is a constant times X^{5/6}.

Combining the eligibility count with Theorem 1.6 gives Theorem 1.8: the number of GL_2(Z)-classes of irreducible binary quartic forms per eligible (I,J) with a given number of real roots tends to 2 zeta(2)/n_i, with n_0 = 4, n_1 = n_2 = 2, i.e. zeta(2)/2 for 4 real roots and zeta(2) otherwise.
acceptance: Height-change check: replacing H by H' multiplies the count constants by (27/4)^{5/6}; ST.0's acceptance condition ('changing height changes the theorem until a comparison is proved') is met here by the explicit relation 27H = 4H'.

Stabilizer weight check: the automorphism weights n_0 = 4, n_1 = n_2 = 2 in Theorem 1.8 are the orders of the stabilizers in the three real cases and must be carried; see the node on the parametrization, where the stabilizer is identified with E(K)[2].
Eligibility check: test (I,J) = (1,2) (eligible, case b) and (I,J) = (1,0) (not eligible), and verify against a direct search for integral forms.
Check the X^{5/6} order: H(I,J) < X means |I| < X^{1/3} and |J| < 2 X^{1/2}, giving about X^{1/3 + 1/2} = X^{5/6} pairs.

sources.locator: Section 2, formulas (3)-(6), printed p. 6; Theorem 1.7, printed pp. 4-5; section 1.1 and section 3 opening, printed pp. 1 and 22

nodes.title: The Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer/Cremona parametrization: 2-Selmer elements as locally soluble integral binary quartic forms
nodes.statement: (Theorem 3.2) Let K have characteristic not 2 or 3 and E : y^2 = x^3 - (I/3) x - J/27 over K. There is a bijection between E(K)/2E(K) and PGL_2(K)-orbits of K-soluble binary quartic forms with invariants I and J, given explicitly by (xi, eta) + 2E(K) |-> PGL_2(K) . ( (1/4) x^4 - (3/2) xi x^2 y^2 + 2 eta x y^3 + (I/3 - (3/4) xi^2) y^4 ); the identity element corresponds to the orbit of forms having a linear factor over K; and the stabilizer in PGL_2(K) of ANY binary quartic form in V_K with nonzero discriminant and invariants I, J is isomorphic to E(K)[2]. (Proposition 3.3) Over Q, isomorphism classes of locally soluble 2-coverings of E correspond to PGL_2(Q)-orbits of locally soluble binary quartic forms with invariants I, J, the rational forms with a rational linear factor forming one orbit that corresponds to the identity of the 2-Selmer group. (Lemma 3.4 and Theorem 3.5) If f is locally soluble with integral invariants I, J satisfying (2^4 . 3) | I and (2^6 . 3^3) | J, then f is PGL_2(Q)-equivalent to an INTEGRAL form; consequently the elements of S_2(E^{I,J}) correspond bijectively to PGL_2(Q)-classes of locally soluble INTEGRAL binary quartic forms with invariants 2^4 I and 2^6 J, the identity corresponding to the class of forms with a rational linear factor.
hypotheses: char K not 2 and not 3; K-soluble means z^2 = f(x,y) has a solution with x,y,z in K and (x,y) != (0,0)
Locally soluble means R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every prime p
The rescaling to invariants 2^4 I and 2^6 J is forced by Lemma 3.4's divisibility hypothesis; the correspondence is NOT between S_2(E^{I,J}) and forms of invariants I, J over Z
The stabilizer identification holds for any form of nonzero discriminant, soluble or not, and is what supplies the automorphism weights in the counting argument

SOURCE STATUS: Theorem 3.2's first paragraph is quoted from Cremona-Fisher-Stoll [16, Prop 2.2] and the second from Cremona [15, sections 3-5, Remark 1]; Proposition 3.3 is quoted from Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer [9, Lemma 2 ff.]; Lemma 3.4 from [9, Lemmas 3, 4, 5]. None of these proofs is given in the source read.
proofSteps: The source collects the classical correspondence and states precisely the three ingredients it needs: the K-level bijection with the explicit formula, the global 2-covering statement, and the integrality lemma.

Theorem 3.5 is deduced by combining Proposition 3.3 with Lemma 3.4 after replacing E^{I,J} by the isomorphic curve y^2 = x^3 - (2^4 I(E)/3) x - 2^6 J(E)/27, which makes the divisibility hypotheses of Lemma 3.4 automatic.
PROOF BOUNDARY: the proofs of Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3 and Lemma 3.4 are in [16], [15] and [9] and were not read.
acceptance: Inverse map check: ST.1's acceptance condition requires a proved inverse for the orbit-to-object bijection. The source gives the forward map explicitly, but the inverse (recovering (xi, eta) from an orbit) is in the quoted references and was not read here.
Stabilizer check: the stabilizer is E(K)[2], of order 1, 2 or 4 over R according to the number of real roots; this is exactly the source of the weights n_0 = 4, n_1 = n_2 = 2 in Theorem 1.8.

Identity-element check: the class of forms with a rational linear factor is a single orbit and must be excluded when counting NONIDENTITY Selmer elements; this is why the counting problem is about IRREDUCIBLE forms.
Scaling check: verify the factors 2^4 and 2^6 on a worked curve; dropping them makes the integral count count the wrong set.

sources.locator: Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Lemma 3.4, Theorem 3.5, printed pp. 22-23
sources.excerpt: Theorem 3.5 Let E = E^{I,J} be an elliptic curve over Q. Then the elements of the 2-Selmer group of E are in one-to-one correspondence with PGL_2(Q)-equivalence classes of locally soluble integral binary quartic forms having invariants equal to 2^4 I and 2^6 J. Furthermore, the set of integral binary quartic forms that have a rational linear factor and invariants equal to 2^4 I and 2^6 J lie in one PGL_2(Q)-equivalence class, and this class corresponds to the identity element in the 2-Selmer group of E.
sources.match: The exact global statement used by the counting argument, with the rescaled invariants and the identification of the identity class.

sources.excerpt: Furthermore, the stabilizer in PGL_2(K) of any (not necessarily K-soluble) binary quartic form f in V_K, having nonzero discriminant and invariants I and J, is isomorphic to E(K)[2], where E is the elliptic curve defined by y^2 = x^3 - (I/3) x - J/27.
sources.match: The stabilizer identification required by ST.1's acceptance condition and used for the automorphism weights.

nodes.title: Theorem 2.14 and Proposition 2.16: the auxiliary embedding of binary quartic orbits into pairs of ternary quadratic forms
nodes.statement: There is a map phi from V_Z (integral binary quartic forms) to W_{Z,1} (a slice of the space W_Z of pairs of integral ternary quadratic forms) inducing a canonical bijection between PGL_2(Z)-orbits on V_Z and F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-orbits on W_{Z,1}, and hence a natural map psi : PGL_2(Z)\V_Z -> (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z. An element of (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z with nonzero discriminant has at most 12 preimages under psi. Interpreted via the ring-theoretic dictionaries, (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z parametrizes pairs (Q,R) with Q a quartic ring and R a cubic resolvent ring, PGL_2(Z)\V_Z parametrizes triples (Q,R,x) with R monogenic and x a monogenizer, and psi forgets the monogenizer.
hypotheses: The PGL_2 action on V used here is the twisted one gamma . f(x,y) = (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma); the PGL_2(Z)-orbits on V_Z coincide with the GL_2(Z)-orbits because -Id acts trivially
The bound of 12 preimages requires nonzero discriminant
The ring-theoretic interpretations are quoted: (Q,R) from Bhargava's higher composition laws [3], the (Q,R,x) description from Wood [44]
proofSteps: The map phi is defined by (30) of the source and is checked to be equivariant: phi(gamma . f) and rho(gamma) . phi(f) agree in F_{Z,1}\W_{Z,1}.

Proposition 2.16 is proved by reducing, via Theorem 2.14, to bounding the number of F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-inequivalent preimages in W_{Z,1} of a fixed w, using the associated monic integral binary cubic forms g_alpha(x,y) = (1/4) Det(A_1 x - B_alpha y), which all have x^3-coefficient 1 and are pairwise inequivalent.
PURPOSE: the source introduces this embedding solely to transport a previously proved uniformity estimate on W_Z (Theorem 2.19, quoted from [4, Proposition 23]) to V_Z; see the uniformity node.
acceptance: Check the 12: it is the bound actually used in deducing Theorem 2.20 from Theorem 2.19, so an implementation must not weaken it to 'finitely many'.
Check the equivariance of phi before using the orbit bijection.
Check that the ring-theoretic reading is a quoted interpretation, not something proved in this source.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.14 The map phi defined by (30) gives a canonical bijection between PGL_2(Z)-orbits on V_Z and F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-orbits on W_{Z,1}. ... Proposition 2.16 An element of (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z with nonzero discriminant has at most 12 preimages in PGL_2(Z)\V_Z under the map psi.
sources.match: The orbit bijection and the finite-fibre bound, with the nonzero-discriminant hypothesis, exactly as stated in the node.

nodes.title: Theorem 2.5, Davenport's lattice-point estimate and the cusp cutoff
nodes.statement: (Theorem 2.5) For any GL_2(Z)-invariant S contained in V_Z^{(i)}, N(S;X) = (1/C_{G_0}^{(i)}) integral over g in N'(t) A' Lambda of #{x in S^{irr} cap B(n,t,lambda,X)} t^{-2} dn d^x t d^x lambda, where B(n,t,lambda,X) = n^{t^{-1}} a_t lambda G_0 . L cap {x in V_R : H(x) < X}. (Proposition 2.6, Davenport) For a bounded semialgebraic multiset R in R^n of maximum multiplicity m defined by at most k polynomial inequalities of degree at most l, the number of integral lattice points in R counted with multiplicity is Vol(R) + O(max{Vol(R-bar), 1}) where Vol(R-bar) is the largest d-dimensional volume of a projection of R onto a coordinate subspace, 1 <= d <= n-1, the implied constant depending only on n, m, k, l. (Proposition 2.7) The number of lattice points (a,b,c,d,e) in B(n,t,lambda,X) with a != 0 is 0 if C lambda < t, and Vol(B(n,t,lambda,X)) + O(t^4 lambda^{16}) otherwise. (Lemmas 2.3, 2.4) Reducible forms are confined to the cusp: the number of GL_2(Z)-orbits of integral binary quartic forms with nonzero discriminant, bounded height and reducible over Q is of strictly smaller order than the main term.
hypotheses: The fundamental domain is not compact: it has a cuspidal region going off to infinity, and the entire difficulty is that lattice points must be counted there

Proposition 2.6 is stated by Davenport for compact semialgebraic sets; the source records that the general bounded semialgebraic multiset case follows by partitioning into constant-multiplicity pieces and applying the result to closures and boundaries

In Proposition 2.7, C is a fixed constant with C^4 bounding the absolute values of all coefficients of all forms in G_0 . L; the bound depends on the choice of the compact set G_0 and the fixed set of representatives L
The integrand in (16) is nonzero only when t <= C lambda and lambda < X^{1/24}, which is what makes the t- and lambda-integrals converge
proofSteps: Reduction theory (section 2.1) produces fundamental domains for GL_2(Z) acting on V_R^{(i)} as finite covers of a translate of a Siegel-type domain; averaging over a compact G_0 in GL_2(R) turns the count of orbits into the integral (16).

The key geometric input in the cusp is Proposition 2.7: in the region C lambda < t there are NO lattice points with a != 0, because |a| <= C^4 lambda^4/t^4 < 1; and outside it the coefficient bounds |a| <= C^4 lambda^4/t^4, |b| <= C^4 lambda^4/t^2, |c| <= C^4 lambda^4, |d| <= C^4 lambda^4 t^2, |e| <= C^4 lambda^4 t^4 give the projection bound O(t^4 lambda^{16}).
Lemmas 2.3 and 2.4 show the points with a = 0 (the cusp) are reducible and negligible, so the count of IRREDUCIBLE orbits equals the volume plus the stated error.
The volumes are computed in section 2.4, yielding the constants 4/135, 32/135, 8/135 times zeta(2) in Theorem 2.1 and the error O(X^{3/4 + epsilon}).
PROOF BOUNDARY: section 2.1 (reduction theory) and section 2.4 (volume computations) were not read.
acceptance: Cusp check: verify that in the region C lambda < t the leading coefficient a must vanish; this is the precise mechanism by which 'the cusp contains only reducible points'.
Error-term check: the error in Theorem 2.1 is O(X^{3/4 + epsilon}) against a main term X^{5/6}; 3/4 < 5/6, so the count is genuinely asymptotic.

Davenport check: Proposition 2.6's error is the largest PROJECTION volume, not the surface area; the projection bound O(t^4 lambda^{16}) in Proposition 2.7 is computed by dropping the smallest of the five coefficient ranges.

Multiplicity check: N(S;X) counts EQUIVALENCE CLASSES, and the averaging formula divides by the measure of the compact averaging set; stabilizer orders enter through C_{G_0}^{(i)} = n_i integral_{G_0} dh.

Proposition 2.7 The number of lattice points (a,b,c,d,e) in B(n,t,lambda,X) with a != 0 is 0 if C lambda < t; Vol(B(n,t,lambda,X)) + O(t^4 lambda^{16}) otherwise.
sources.match: The averaging formula and the cusp cutoff with the exact threshold and error, as summarized in the node.

sources.locator: Proposition 2.6 and the paragraph following it, printed p. 11
sources.excerpt: Proposition 2.6 Let R be a bounded, semialgebraic multiset in R^n having maximum multiplicity m, and that is defined by at most k polynomial inequalities each having degree at most l. Then the number of integral lattice points (counted with multiplicity) contained in the region R is Vol(R) + O(max{Vol(R-bar), 1}) ... Davenport states the above proposition only for the number of lattice points in compact semialgebraic sets R subset R^n.

nodes.title: Theorem 2.13: a uniform tail estimate permitting the sieve to infinitely many congruence conditions
nodes.statement: For a prime p let W_p(V) be the set of integral binary quartic forms f with p^2 | Delta(f). Then for any M > 0, lim_{X -> infinity} N(union_{p > M} W_p(V); X) / X^{5/6} = O(1/log M), with the implied constant independent of M.
hypotheses: The estimate is uniform in M: the implied constant does not depend on M, which is exactly what licenses interchanging the sieve limit with the height limit
It is a statement about GL_2(Z)-orbit counts N( . ; X), not about raw lattice-point counts
The bound 1/log M tends to 0 as M -> infinity, but only logarithmically
proofSteps: The proof embeds V_Z into W_Z (pairs of integral ternary quadratic forms) via the map psi of Theorem 2.14, using Proposition 2.16 (at most 12 preimages) to transfer counts.
On W_Z the corresponding uniformity estimate is Theorem 2.19, quoted from [4, Proposition 23] (Bhargava, 'The density of discriminants of quartic rings and fields'), which was NOT read.
Transporting it back through psi gives Theorem 2.20 and then Theorem 2.13.

The estimate is combined with Theorems 2.11 and 2.12 (counting with finitely many congruence conditions) to give Theorem 2.21, the sieve to acceptable functions defined by infinitely many congruence conditions.
PROOF BOUNDARY: the proofs of Theorems 2.17-2.21 were not read; only their statements and the role of Theorem 2.14/Proposition 2.16.
acceptance: Interchange check: ST.2's acceptance condition says an interchange of sieve and height limits needs a uniform tail theorem, not pointwise densities. Theorem 2.13 is exactly that theorem; check that the constant's independence from M is carried.
Squarefree-discriminant check: the intended application is counting forms of squarefree discriminant, obtained by excluding union_p W_p(V).
Order check: the tail is O(X^{5/6}/log M), i.e. of the same order as the main term divided by log M; it does not beat the main term for fixed M.

sources.locator: Section 2.6, Theorem 2.13 and the paragraph explaining the method, printed p. 15
sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.13 For a prime p, let W_p(V) denote the set of binary quartic forms f in V_Z such that p^2 | Delta(f). Then, for any M > 0, we have: lim_{X->infinity} N(union_{p>M} W_p(V); X)/X^{5/6} = O(1/log M), where the implied constant is independent of M. ... to prove this estimate, we use the following trick. We embed the space of integral binary quartic forms into the space of pairs of integral ternary quadratic forms, where such an estimate has been proven previously [4, Proposition 23].
sources.match: The uniformity statement with the independence of the constant, and the source's own identification of the imported estimate and the embedding trick.

nodes.title: The quadratic and cubic predecessors (Mertens/Siegel and Davenport), quoted without proof in this source
nodes.statement: (Theorem 1.4, Mertens 1874 / Siegel 1944) With h_D the number of SL_2(Z)-classes of irreducible integral binary quadratic forms of discriminant D: sum_{-X < D < 0} h_D ~ (pi/18) X^{3/2}, and sum_{0 < D < X} h_D log eps_D ~ (pi^2/18) X^{3/2}, where eps_D = (t + u sqrt(D))/2 with t, u the smallest positive integral solutions of t^2 - D u^2 = 4. (Theorem 1.5, Davenport 1951) With h(D) the number of GL_2(Z)-classes of irreducible integral binary cubic forms of discriminant D: sum_{-X < D < 0} h(D) ~ (pi^2/24) X and sum_{0 < D < X} h(D) ~ (pi^2/72) X. Via Delone-Faddeev, classes of irreducible integral binary cubic forms correspond to orders in cubic fields, so Theorem 1.5 counts cubic orders by discriminant.
hypotheses: h_D is the narrow class number and log eps_D the regulator of the unique quadratic order of discriminant D; the real case is a class-number-times-regulator statement, NOT a class-number statement
The cubic statement is about GL_2(Z)-classes, and irreducibility is required; reducible forms are excluded
The Delone-Faddeev correspondence is with ORDERS in cubic fields (including non-maximal ones), not with cubic fields
IMPORT STATUS: neither theorem is proved in the source read; they are quoted as the classical predecessors of Theorem 1.6, with references [18] (Davenport) and the Mertens/Siegel attribution
proofSteps: No proof is given in the source read. The statements are recorded here because ST.3's acceptance condition requires the count to fix the degree, Galois group and automorphism weights, and these two theorems are the exact low-degree cases with which any ST.3 development must agree.

Next source action recorded in this packet's gaps: read Davenport, 'On a principle of Lipschitz' and 'On the class-number of binary cubic forms I/II' (1951), and Siegel's 1944 paper, or a modern exposition.
acceptance: Consistency check: Theorem 1.6 (quartic) has main term of order X^{5/6} in the height, while Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 have X^{3/2} and X in the discriminant; the orderings are by different invariants and must not be compared directly.
Weight check: the quadratic count is by SL_2(Z)-classes, the cubic and quartic counts by GL_2(Z)-classes; the group must be recorded.
Regulator check: in the real quadratic case the sum is weighted by log eps_D, and no unweighted asymptotic for h_D alone is asserted.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 1.5 with the surrounding interpretation, printed pp. 3-4
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.4 (Mertens 1874/Siegel 1944) ... (a) sum_{-X<D<0} h_D ~ (pi/18) X^{3/2}; (b) sum_{0<D<X} h_D log eps_D ~ (pi^2/18) X^{3/2} ... Theorem 1.5 (Davenport 1951) ... (a) sum_{-X<D<0} h(D) ~ (pi^2/24) X; (b) sum_{0<D<X} h(D) ~ (pi^2/72) X.
sources.match: Verbatim statements with the exact constants and weights; the node records that no proof appears in this source.

nodes.title: Theorem 3.1: the average size of S_2(E) over any large family is 3, via a Tamagawa-number evaluation
nodes.statement: Call a family F of elliptic curves over Q defined by congruence conditions LARGE if, for all but finitely many p, Inv_p(F) contains every (I,J) in Z_p x Z_p with p^2 not dividing Delta(I,J). Then, when the curves of any large family are ordered by height, the average size of the 2-Selmer group S_2(E) is 3. The family of all elliptic curves, every family cut out by finitely many congruence conditions on the coefficients, and the family of all semistable elliptic curves are all large. The proof evaluates the average of #S_2(E) - 1 as Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R)) prod_p Vol(PGL_2(Z_p)), which equals 2 zeta(2) prod_p (1 - p^{-2}) = 2, the Tamagawa number of PGL_2 over Q.
hypotheses: F must be LARGE, not merely defined by congruence conditions; largeness allows infinitely many conditions but requires that at all but finitely many p nothing is excluded away from p^2 | Delta
The average is over the ordering by height H' (equivalently H); a different ordering is a different theorem
Proposition 3.18 (if f is bad at p > 2, i.e. not Q_p-soluble or m_p(f) != 1, then p^2 | Delta(f)) is what makes the local conditions compatible with largeness

nodes.title: Corollary 1.2: average 2-Selmer rank at most 1.5, and why this does not compute the Mordell-Weil rank
nodes.statement: From the exact sequence 0 -> E(Q)/2E(Q) -> S_2(E) -> Sha_E[2] -> 0 one gets r_2(S_2(E)) = r(E) + r_2(E(Q)[2]) + r_2(Sha_E[2]). Using the elementary inequality 2 r_2(S_2(E)) <= 2^{r_2(S_2(E))} = |S_2(E)| and Theorem 1.1, the mean of the left-hand side is at most 1.5, hence so is the mean of each of r(E), r_2(E(Q)[2]) and r_2(Sha_E[2]) separately. Since 0% of elliptic curves have rational 2-torsion, the mean of r_2(E(Q)[2]) is 0. Therefore the limsup of the average rank of all elliptic curves over Q, ordered by height, is at most 1.5.
hypotheses: The three summands on the right of the rank identity are non-negative, which is what allows each mean to be bounded by the mean of the sum
The inequality 2x <= 2^x holds for all non-negative integers x and is where the loss from 'average size 3' to 'average rank at most 1.5' occurs
The conclusion is about the LIMSUP of the average rank; no lower bound and no limit is asserted
The Mordell-Weil rank is bounded, not computed: the bound holds because r_2(Sha_E[2]) >= 0, and nothing here controls Sha
proofSteps: Write the 2-descent exact sequence (1) and take F_2-dimensions to get (2).
Apply 2 r_2(S_2) <= 2^{r_2(S_2)} = |S_2| pointwise, then average and use Theorem 1.1 to bound the mean of |S_2| by 3.
Conclude mean r_2(S_2(E)) <= 3/2; since the three terms in (2) are non-negative, each has mean at most 3/2.
Note that the mean of r_2(E(Q)[2]) is 0 because a density 0 set of curves has rational 2-torsion (asserted as elementary in the source, not proved there).
acceptance: ST.4's acceptance condition is met exactly here: the Selmer average bounds the rank through the convexity inequality 2x <= 2^x, and the Selmer rank is NOT equated with the Mordell-Weil rank; the gap is r_2(Sha_E[2]), which is not controlled.
Check the loss: if all Selmer groups had size exactly 3 the rank bound would still be 1.5 rather than log_2(3) ~ 1.585 or the conjectured 0.5; the inequality is lossy and this must be recorded.
Check that the 2-torsion term is handled by a density statement and not by an inequality.
Check the direction: Theorem 1.1 is an equality (average exactly 3), Corollary 1.2 only an upper bound for ranks.

Indeed, note that Equation (1) implies that r_2(S_2(E)) = r(E) + r_2(E(Q)[2]) + r_2(Sha_E[2]), where ... Due to the inequality 2 r_2(S_2(E)) <= 2^{r_2(S_2(E))} = |S_2(E)|, Theorem 1.1 bounds the mean of the left hand side of (2) by 1.5, and thus the same bound holds also for the average size of each of the terms on the right hand side of (2).
